name: zzuf
why: A transparent input fuzzer that mutates file bytes under a program is a classic door into how software breaks on malformed input.

brief.what_it_is: zzuf is a transparent application input fuzzer. It runs a target program and corrupts the data that program reads, by intercepting file and network operations and flipping random bits in the input. The program then sees malformed input, and crashes or memory faults it hits are the output. The Homebrew entry lists two executables, zzuf and zzat. The homepage is an old Trac wiki page; the README is short and sends readers to the wiki and manual page for usage.
brief.why_it_exists: The author frames it as a way to find bugs in applications by corrupting user-supplied data, which often comes from untrusted sources on the Internet. The homepage says the idea of fuzzing is barely new, and the main goal is to make it easier and automated.
brief.how_it_works: zzuf intercepts file and network operations and changes random bits in the program's input. Its behaviour is deterministic, so a bug found with a given seed can be reproduced. The homepage lists three uses: quality assurance and test suites, security (segfaults and memory corruption as possible holes), and code coverage analysis.
brief.install_notes: Downloads are on GitHub releases (https://github.com/samhocevar/zzuf/releases). The tutorial says it requires zzuf 0.11 or later. Nothing else about accounts, runtimes, or first-run configuration appeared in the pages I read.
brief.standout: zzuf is aimed at real-world targets such as media players, image viewers and web browsers, rather than only unit tests. It is transparent: the target program is not modified, because the tool intercepts its I/O. The homepage says CERT's Basic Fuzzing Framework (BFF) is based on it.
brief.status: unknown. The Trac wiki page says it was last modified on 06/09/2015. The GitHub README has a Travis CI badge but no release or commit date showed in what I fetched. The tutorial is marked WORK IN PROGRESS.
brief.caveats: Support is listed as: Linux (glibc), FreeBSD, OpenBSD, Mac OS X and OpenSolaris fully supported; NetBSD almost working; Windows not ready. The tutorial is marked WORK IN PROGRESS, and its advanced sections are only partly described on the pages I read. The homepage notes that zzuf is full of black magic and difficult to hack on. Licensing was not visible in the pages I read.

zzuf's behaviour is deterministic, making it easy to reproduce bugs.
zzuf is not rocket science: the idea of fuzzing input data is barely new, but zzuf's main purpose is to make things easier and automated.

judge.reason: Its transparent, deterministic mutation of real programs’ file and network input makes fuzzing tangible without modifying the target.

entry.title: zzuf
entry.tldr: A fuzzer that sits under any program and flips random bits in the data it reads, so you can watch software break on malformed input.
entry.deeper_look:
zzuf runs a target program and corrupts what that program reads. It intercepts file and network operations and flips random bits in the input. The program is not modified or recompiled. It simply receives damaged data, and the crashes or memory faults that follow are the output.

The author's motivation is that much of the data applications handle comes from untrusted sources on the Internet, and corrupting it is a cheap way to find bugs. The homepage is modest about it: "zzuf is not rocket science: the idea of fuzzing input data is barely new, but zzuf's main purpose is to make things easier and automated."

The idea underneath is deterministic fuzzing. zzuf's behaviour is deterministic, so a bug found with a given seed can be reproduced. That turns random breakage into something you can investigate. The homepage lists three uses: quality assurance and test suites, security work (segfaults and memory corruption as possible holes), and code coverage analysis.

It is aimed at real-world targets such as media players, image viewers and web browsers, not only unit tests. The homepage says CERT's Basic Fuzzing Framework (BFF) is based on it. Two executables are installed: zzuf, and zzat.

entry.whats_unique: It is transparent: the target program is untouched because zzuf intercepts its I/O, and runs are seeded so any crash can be reproduced.
entry.caveats: The homepage wiki was last modified in 2015, the tutorial is marked work in progress, and the author warns the code is full of black magic and hard to hack on.
